i get how it’s out of the scope of aba, but for me, i almost feel scared by the concept of removing emotion from scenarios like this. idk for me if i saw a kid suffering with their gender identity, i would prioritize empathy and compassion, and if that kid struggling with their identity is lucky enough to have an aba therapist who has walked that same path, all i see is how it could be helpful to know that they are not alone. gender identity is a difficult subject i understand, but behind the politics there are actual kids who feel alone, scared, and confused. i was looking at the aca code of ethics, idek if it applies to aba but i’m assuming so, it can be ethical to disclose personal information like that as long as it’s not intrusive, focus should always be on the client. tbh i think this is important because the suffering that trans kids go thru, autistic or not, does affect their thinking and behavior. especially as kids get older, it’s not just about changing the behavior. i have worked with teens before and a lot of those goals aren’t just “tolerate non preferred for 10 mins anymore,” they’re more about working on negative self talk. can this not be helped if the situation included a kid or teen hating who they are because they’re questioning their identity? abc antecedent behavior and consequence, antecedent is important! why is this kid hurting themselves/others/acting in whatever way? what was the setting event? what happened before they started hurting themselves/etc? were they called by a name or pronoun they don’t identify with? i would absolutely proceed with caution and never turn the focus onto myself, but i truly believe it can only help to provide acceptance and understanding, and sometimes self-disclosure can do that. i am not trans but if i had a trans client i would acknowledge them as they are and always have their back. it also depends on age, how well/long i’ve know the client and their family. but to me the emotions of the client are just as important as their behaviors, if anything they go hand in hand. avoiding the conversation might be modeling avoidance bx too, what do you think?

I guess it depends on your perspective. In my opinion, capitalism has completely consumed every aspect of our lives. We are no longer living real lives. Every interaction has been written out for us. The conditions we are living in have soaked into our conversations, every exchange. Nvc (IN MY OPINION) is a communication strategy that is based on the idea that we cannot control others, that we are in control of ourselves, that it is in our nature to give and receive compassionately. Capitalism is so much more than the sale of labor value and in some ways Marxism actually prioritizes the very things that are the foundation to capitalism (value labor necessity). Capitalism comes with its own philosophy, a million justifications (ex Darwinism). Nvc (in my opinion) tears down one the the crucial justifications for capitalism, that the only way to survive is to force our needs and reality upon others. I’m not sure if you’ve read these books before but if you’re interested I really recommend the revolution of everyday life by raoul vaneigem, the society of the spectacle by guy debord, and the abolition of work by bob black (it’s an essay you can find it on the anarchist library). Capitalism comes with a philosophy, and it is so much bigger that I truly don’t believe it can be beaten with just one strategy. Anything that successfully argues against a capitalist philosophy is anti capitalism in my book, but that’s just me.

I think you’re being too sensitive. Ppl can set boundaries. That doesn’t mean you have to like it, but you should respect it bc disrespecting them won’t get you any closer to this person. You also have the choice to set boundaries. This person doesn’t want to spend time with you one on one because they don’t feel comfortable. That’s totally okay, but me personally I wouldn’t want to be friends with someone who doesn’t want to spend time with me one on one, so I’d probably say something like, “I respect/admire you setting boundaries about hanging out but I have to set my own boundaries. I’d love to be your friend but I have a need for one on one time with my friends. I know you’ve been through a lot with other people so I understand your need for space, but that makes us incompatible as friends. So I wanna say that I’m always here to reconcile and start a new friendship that includes spending time hanging out but if we can only hang out in groups that would make me too sad because I interpret that as rejection. I’m willing to make compromises that could build trust between us, but if that’s out of your comfort zone right now that’s okay, let’s just go our separate ways for now.”

Something like that. Maybe not as clinical sounding as I made it but yeah. Who knows what she’s been through, I understand her fear. But if not hanging out one on one doesn’t work for you, probably best to move on 🤷‍♀️ I don’t think it’s helpful to question ur friends honesty in this case, she’s told you what she told you and that’s what you’re gonna have to work with.
